quests.hint: After hours of searching the office for the missing employee, the security team realised his keycard had been used to exit the building three hours earlier, making his claim of being inside all day impossible. Which idiom describes what the evidence showed?
quests.explanation: 'The game is up' means that deception or wrongdoing has been discovered and cannot continue. Example: 'When the CCTV footage was examined, the game was up — there was no credible denial left.' It implies that pretence or concealment is no longer possible.

quests.hint: Despite having a well-paid, stable job, Mark constantly envied colleagues who worked in startups — convinced their chaotic, uncertain life was more exciting than his own comfortable routine. Which idiom describes his thinking?
quests.explanation: 'The grass is always greener on the other side' means other people's situations always seem better or more desirable than your own, even when they may not be. Example: 'She wanted a corporate job when she had freelance freedom, and vice versa — the grass is always greener.' It warns against idealistic comparisons.
options: every cloud has a silver lining
the grass is always greener on the other side
you can't have your cake and eat it too

quests.hint: A colleague asked you to briefly explain the current financial situation without going into lengthy detail. You provide a concise summary covering the essentials. Which idiom describes what you are giving them?
quests.explanation: 'The long and the short of it' means the essential summary or conclusion of a matter, without all the lengthy detail. Example: 'The long and the short of it is that we don't have enough money to proceed this quarter.' It promises the listener the essential point without time-consuming elaboration.
options: the long and the short of it

quests.hint: The birthday party already had twenty confirmed guests, but when the host said there was still room, the friends agreed that having more people would only make the celebration livelier and more fun. Which idiom expresses this view?
quests.explanation: 'The more the merrier' means that the more people or things there are involved, the better and more enjoyable the situation will be. Example: 'Invite your colleagues too — the more the merrier!' It expresses the idea that greater quantity or company is always welcome.
options: too many cooks spoil the broth

quests.hint: The minister admitted that the corruption scandal involving three officials was serious, but investigators privately believed it involved dozens more across multiple departments. Which idiom describes what the scandal might represent?
quests.explanation: 'The tip of the iceberg' means a small, visible portion of a much larger, mostly hidden problem. Example: 'The cases we know about are just the tip of the iceberg — the full extent of the fraud is far greater.' It comes from the fact that only around ten percent of an iceberg is visible above the waterline.

quests.hint: After several unsuccessful formulas, the chemistry student tried a slightly different combination, failed again, adjusted again, and gradually worked her way toward an effective compound over many iterations. Which idiom describes her method?
quests.explanation: 'Trial and error' means a method of solving problems by trying various approaches and learning from each failure until one succeeds. Example: 'The recipe was developed entirely through trial and error over two years of testing.' It is a fundamental approach to learning and problem-solving.

quests.hint: Throughout the entire case, the defence seemed to be losing, and the prosecution appeared confident. But in the final hour, new evidence emerged that completely reversed the situation in the defendant's favour. Which idiom describes what happened?
quests.explanation: 'Turn the tables' means to completely reverse a situation so that the person who was at a disadvantage suddenly gains the upper hand. Example: 'The underdog team turned the tables in the final quarter and won convincingly.' It comes from the image of literally turning a game table around to exchange positions.

quests.hint: For decades, every career decision the vice president made was dictated by the demands and preferences of the founder, who maintained absolute control over everything she did professionally. Which idiom describes her professional situation?
quests.explanation: 'Under someone's thumb' means completely controlled or dominated by another person, with little or no autonomy. Example: 'He's entirely under his manager's thumb — he can't make a single decision independently.' It comes from the image of someone being physically held down by another's thumb.

quests.hint: The executive who had spent years undermining colleagues and backstabbing rivals was eventually fired by the very team he had manipulated, using tactics he had taught them himself. Which idiom captures this outcome?
quests.explanation: 'What goes around comes around' means that the actions you take — good or bad — will eventually return to affect you in kind. Example: 'He treated his team with contempt for years, and what goes around comes around — they unanimously voted against renewing his contract.' It implies karma and moral justice.
options: every cloud has a silver lining

quests.hint: The research team had spent six months working on a solution, but every possible technical avenue had now been exhausted without success, leaving them completely stuck. Which idiom describes their situation?
quests.explanation: 'Hit a brick wall' means to encounter a complete obstacle or barrier that prevents any further progress. Example: 'We've hit a brick wall on the development side — we need entirely new expertise to move forward.' It uses the image of a solid wall that physically stops forward movement.

quests.hint: After months of strategic planning and high-level discussion, the team agreed it was time to stop talking and actually begin doing the difficult practical work required to implement the plan. Which idiom describes this shift?
quests.explanation: 'Roll up your sleeves' means to prepare to do hard, practical work after a period of planning or delay. Example: 'The strategy is agreed — now it's time to roll up our sleeves and implement it.' It comes from the literal action of rolling up shirt sleeves before manual or physical labour.
options: took the path of least resistance

quests.hint: Remote working gave employees more family time and reduced commuting stress, but it also weakened team cohesion and made informal mentoring much harder. Which idiom captures this complexity?
quests.explanation: 'Cut both ways' means to have both positive and negative effects or implications at the same time. Example: 'The new policy cuts both ways — it benefits experienced staff but disadvantages newcomers.' It comes from the image of a blade that cuts in either direction.
options: the proof is in the pudding

quests.hint: After the company's founder retired, the new leadership team was expected to uphold the company's founding values and continue the mission that had been established over thirty years. Which idiom describes the new team's responsibility?
quests.explanation: 'Carry the torch' means to continue a tradition, cause, or mission that was started by someone else, especially after they have stepped back. Example: 'The next generation of scientists must carry the torch of this important research.' It comes from the image of runners passing a burning torch in a relay race.

quests.hint: Unable to attend the industry dinner on Thursday, the senior partner asked her colleague to accept the invitation on her behalf and attend in her place instead. Which idiom applies to her own situation?
quests.explanation: 'Take a rain check' means to decline an invitation or offer now but express willingness to accept it at a future time. Example: 'I can't make it tonight, but can I take a rain check for next week?' It comes from American baseball, where a rain check was issued to fans allowing them to attend a postponed match later.

quests.hint: The generous grant came with a strict requirement that all funded research must be published exclusively in the foundation's own journal, giving the foundation control over the findings. Which idiom describes the grant?
quests.explanation: 'Come with strings attached' means to involve hidden conditions, requirements, or obligations that must be met in exchange for the apparent benefit. Example: 'The investment came with strings attached — they demanded a seat on the board.' It comes from the image of a puppet controlled by strings.
options: was a gift from the universe

quests.hint: When the experienced goalkeeper was injured, the backup goalkeeper — who had never played in a competitive match — had to take full responsibility and perform at the highest level in the critical final. Which idiom describes his situation?
quests.explanation: 'Step up to the plate' means to take on a difficult responsibility or rise to a challenge when it is needed most. Example: 'When the CEO resigned suddenly, the deputy stepped up to the plate and kept the company stable.' It comes from baseball, where a batter must walk to the plate to face the pitch.

quests.hint: By carefully building relationships with the right stakeholders, maintaining consistent performance, and timing her application perfectly, the analyst secured a promotion over more senior colleagues. Which idiom describes her approach?
quests.explanation: 'Play your cards right' means to make the best use of the opportunities and resources you have, taking the right actions to succeed. Example: 'If you play your cards right in this role, you could be a director within five years.' It comes from card games — holding and using your cards wisely to win.

quests.hint: At every networking event, the sales director loudly told everyone who would listen about every major deal he had closed and every prestigious client he had won — without being asked. Which idiom describes his behaviour?
quests.explanation: 'Blow your own trumpet' means to boast openly about your own achievements, often in an embarrassing or annoying way. Example: 'He spends the whole meeting blowing his own trumpet instead of listening to anyone else.' It comes from the idea of playing a fanfare to announce yourself.

quests.hint: With just eight minutes left before the contract had to be signed or the deal would expire permanently, the legal team was still urgently clarifying the final clause. Which idiom describes their timing?
quests.explanation: 'At the eleventh hour' means at the very last possible moment, just before a deadline or opportunity expires. Example: 'The deal was signed at the eleventh hour — just minutes before the option expired.' It comes from the parable of workers hired at the eleventh hour of a twelve-hour working day.
options: at the drop of a hat

quests.hint: After public criticism of individual members, the entire board quickly united and presented a single, unified position to the media, refusing to allow divisions to be exploited by outside pressure. Which idiom describes their action?
quests.explanation: 'Close ranks' means for a group to unite in defence against external criticism or threat, presenting a unified front. Example: 'When the accusations emerged, the company closed ranks and refused all press comment.' It comes from military formations where soldiers draw together to protect the line.

quests.hint: The two co-founders had grown up in the same city, attended the same university, worked in the same industry, and shared almost exactly the same values and management philosophy. Which idiom describes them?
quests.explanation: 'Cut from the same cloth' means very similar in character, background, or values — as though made from the same material. Example: 'The two leaders are cut from the same cloth — both grew up in poverty and built their companies from nothing.' It comes from tailoring, where pieces cut from the same material are identical.

quests.hint: The entire sustainability committee made clear in writing that they categorically opposed the proposal to use single-use plastics, with no conditions, qualifications, or exceptions. Which idiom describes their position?
quests.explanation: 'Dead set against' means completely and firmly opposed to something, with no possibility of being persuaded otherwise. Example: 'The local community is dead set against building a new motorway through the protected woodland.' It implies absolute, unwavering opposition.

quests.hint: Recognising an exceptionally talented young engineer, the department head arranged for her to bypass the standard five-year experience requirement and join the advanced research team directly. Which idiom describes this process?
quests.explanation: 'Fast-track something' means to accelerate something through a process, allowing it to bypass normal stages or timelines to reach completion more quickly. Example: 'The committee agreed to fast-track the planning application given its economic importance.' It suggests a privileged, expedited route.
options: took the path of least resistance

quests.hint: The documentary raised interesting questions about the relationship between artificial intelligence and human creativity that the team had not previously considered and wanted to explore further. Which idiom describes what the documentary provided?
quests.explanation: 'Food for thought' means something that is worth thinking about carefully — an idea, question, or piece of information that stimulates further reflection. Example: 'Her remarks during the lecture gave us all food for thought about the future of education.' It uses the image of nourishment — feeding the mind.

quests.hint: Although the challenger was the heavy underdog, she performed so exceptionally well that she pushed the defending champion to five sets and came extraordinarily close to winning the title. Which idiom describes the challenger's performance?
quests.explanation: 'Give someone a run for their money' means to be so competitive that even though you may not ultimately win, you force the stronger party to work very hard and come close to being beaten. Example: 'The newcomers gave the established firm a real run for their money.' It comes from horse racing.
options: gave them a run for their money

quests.hint: Having ignored every warning from financial advisers and invested the entire company reserve in a single highly speculative venture that collapsed completely, the CEO was dismissed. Which idiom describes the investment outcome?
quests.explanation: 'Go down in flames' means to fail spectacularly and catastrophically, often in a very public way. Example: 'The product launch went down in flames after the technical failures were broadcast live.' It comes from the dramatic image of an aircraft catching fire and plummeting to the ground.

quests.hint: Having secured the exclusive rights to the technology, the company was in a significantly stronger position to set pricing and dictate the terms of any partnership agreement. Which idiom describes the company's position?
quests.explanation: 'Have the upper hand' means to be in a position of advantage or control relative to others in a competition or negotiation. Example: 'With three bidders competing for one contract, the client has the upper hand in negotiations.' It comes from the childhood game of stacking hands on a bat, where the person on top wins.

quests.hint: During the most challenging phase of the crisis, when every team was stretched to its limits and the organisation faced maximum pressure from all directions, the CEO remained visible, calm, and decisive. Which idiom describes her situation?
quests.explanation: 'In the thick of it' means in the middle of the most intense, busiest, or most difficult part of a situation or activity. Example: 'We're right in the thick of the product launch — every day is critical.' It uses 'thick' to suggest density and intensity, like the thick of a forest.

quests.hint: Although negotiations were going well, the experienced diplomat advised her team not to make any final commitments yet and to hold back their strongest argument until the absolute right moment. Which idiom describes her advice?
quests.explanation: 'Keep your powder dry' means to hold back your resources or full effort and save them for when they are most needed. Example: 'Don't spend the entire marketing budget in the first week — keep your powder dry for the peak season.' It comes from the era of gunpowder weapons, where keeping powder dry was essential for battle readiness.

quests.hint: Despite short-term profitability pressures, the board warned against reducing the R&D budget — arguing that cutting the very investment responsible for future products would ultimately end the company's ability to compete. Which idiom describes the board's concern?
quests.explanation: 'Kill the golden goose' means to destroy the source of your own long-term success or wealth by acting greedily or short-sightedly in the short term. Example: 'Cutting the training budget would kill the golden goose — skilled staff are what make this company successful.' It comes from Aesop's fable of the goose that laid golden eggs.
options: struck while the iron was hot
